_what: The Edit Line: the cut and dress stages, one row each, with the owner's open decisions. edit_line_page.py prints the page (context/edit-line.html → the artifact) and its Markdown mirror (EDIT-LINE.md) from this one file. Settle a decision by moving it from `open` to `settled` with his words and the date.

phases.name: Cut
phases.what: Turns the clips into one clean run of picture and sound. Nothing gets added here, it only gets cut and ordered.

stages.name: Trim the dead air
stages.in: Each clip's own sound track. The edit listens to the sound, not the video and not the written-out words.
stages.out: Each clip with its start and end silence gone and its breaths kept. Every longer pause is marked for your review, and every clip that stops mid-line is sent back to production.
rules: Listen first. Silence is found in the sound itself (anything quieter than −35 dB for 0.15s or longer). The written-out words only say WHAT is said. The word tool stretches words across silences and even past the end of a clip, and that broke the an-earlier-run test.
Silence at the start and end of a clip is always cut.
Breaths (pauses under about 0.35s) are always kept. Cutting them makes the voice sound robotic.

Mid-clip pauses (0.35s or longer) are proposed by the machine and checked by you. Some are dead air, and some are a beat that makes the line land (the 2.2s before Nova's “No.” in an-earlier-run clip 6).
After a cut pause, the next piece zooms in 7% so the jump reads like a second camera in the room.
A clip that stops mid-line is an error, not something to edit around. It's marked clearly, goes back to production to be made again, and the production prompt that let it through gets fixed.
stages.bug: Cut from the sound, not the word timings, and the clips-running-past-their-end problem goes away. Before, the breath after the last word was measured from the word tool, which put clip 9's last word at 15.7s on a 14.1s clip.

Reproduce it, clearly marked as an error, and fix it upstream. BUILT 23 Sep. (1) Production's words check now asks whether the line FINISHED, not just whether the words were similar. A cut-off clip is CUT_OFF and never ships. (2) The edit listens to every talking clip before cutting, and a cut-off clip stops the edit and is sent back. settled.q: How is a sent-back clip remade?
settled.answer: Surgically (your words, 23 Sep). Name the broken element and remake only that, then rebuild what depends on it from the same originals. Voice broken: remake that scene's voice slice, then re-clip from the SAME frames with the new voice. Frame broken: fix the frame with one change, then re-clip with the SAME voice. Only the clip broken: re-clip with the same frames and voice. For a cut-off clip the machine listens to the voice slice first to tell which one it is. Two tries at most, then a person.

settled.q: Where is a cut-off line caught?
settled.answer: At production, on the AUDIO, before any picture is paid for (your call, 23 Sep). BUILT: an audio check runs right after the voice is made. Each scene's slice is heard. It must say its line, finish it, and not be silent or clipping. A failing slice is remade once, voice only, then the run stops. The edit's own listen stays only as a backstop. First real test (pigment-memory): every line whole, but the read drifts in volume by 17 LU between scenes (warned, not stopped).

elements_intro: Every element a finished ad can carry. The rule (your words, 23 Sep): the teardown names every element, the brief carries all of them, production makes all of them, and the edit only assembles. At extreme scale each element is a typed, reusable part with an id. The teardown marks it on the swipe's timeline, production makes it once as a file, banks (music, SFX, templates, disclaimers) are made once and reused forever, and the edit becomes a deterministic assembly of parts. A new version is just swapping parts: hook × body × CTA × music × caption look × ratio.

variation.intro: Your words, 23 Sep: “full control of our creative output and variation process down to the word spoken, all the way to pumping out 100 variations at a time with different formats and styles.” The trick at scale: every variation is a set of PARTS. Each part is made once, and the edit assembles combinations for free. Money is spent on parts, never on combinations.

axes.what: The on-screen text from frame one.
The opening visual that stops the thumb.

Swap any section for another version of the same job: hook, identification, problem, agitation, failed solutions, root cause, unique mechanism, solution, product, proof, transformation, objections, offer, urgency, call to action. The vocabulary comes from your marketing doctrine, never a list we made up.
The same parts in a different order: PAS, AIDA, BAB, story/testimonial, mechanism-led, us-vs-them, direct offer, identification-only (the doctrine's ad frameworks).
axes.made: only the sections that framework adds

axes.what: The same film in a different look (the format library's restyle chain: screenplay, blocking and words frozen; only the rendering swaps).
axes.made: re-rendered frames and clips per style

axes.what: A different show format for the same argument.
axes.made: a new production (it changes what the film says)

axes.what: A custom designed cover, not just a frame grab.
Music bed, trend sound, SFX set.

variation.math: Example: 6 hooks × 3 scroll-stoppers × 3 problem sections × 3 unique-mechanism sections × 2 offers = 324 combinations, from 17 parts, and each can run as PAS, mechanism-led or us-vs-them. Add 3 headlines and 2 music beds (free) and it's thousands, still from the same paid parts. The doctrine check removes any combination the awareness level forbids.
rules: The doctrine decides what's allowed. The awareness level decides which sections an ad may use and what the opening must not do (an unaware opening never names the product or price). The sophistication stage decides whether the mechanism leads. Every combination is checked against those rules before it renders, so a bad combo never gets made.
Sections must join cleanly in any order. Each section starts and ends on a shared anchor: the same presenter, wardrobe, setting and a neutral in/out frame. So any opening can sit before any body.
The voice stays one person, one read: each section version is voiced stitched to what plays before it, so the tone never jumps. Then it's heard by the audio gate.
Every part has an id, and every render's name carries its part ids. Spend and results join back to the PART, so you learn which hook, problem or style wins, not just which ad.
Structure is swapped at the section level, never mid-sentence. Words can change inside a section only by making a new version of that section.
No 4:5 and no 1:1. Every render is 9:16.

decisions.q: Which combinations get rendered? All of them, a set number per batch (e.g. 100), or a designed test where each part appears equally often so the results say which PART wins?

Where do the alternative sections come from? The swipe gives one of each, so the extras would be written by the brief stage (new problem angles from the avatar research, new mechanisms from the product file), all from the same research, nothing invented. OK?
Thumbnails: designed covers made at production as their own element (a still with the headline composed on top, like a card), with several per ad?
